Happy birthday to Donald William Kerst, the American physicist who made a significant contribution to accelerator and plasma physics and developed the betatron!

Kerst was born in 1911 in Galena, Illinois. He attended the University of Wisconsin where he earned a PhD in Physics in 1937. After graduation, Kerst researched the development of X-ray technology but struggled to come up with the high energies required, which could not be produced at the time. Later, he moved to the University of Illinois, where he developed the betatron, the first device to accelerate electrons with sufficient momentum as to produce nuclear transformation in atoms using electromagnetic induction.

The betatron influenced all subsequent accelerators, as the high energy X-rays it produces has had extensive applications in the industrial and medical fields to this very day.

I'm now building an "improvements" feature into all of my personal vibecoded applications: a freeform text input that's hooked up to an agent that yolo implements whatever is submitted.

It's an interesting experience -- the activation energy barrier to sanding any rough edge or implementing any new feature becomes extremely low. Someone else who uses one of the applications I created has already implemented 150 improvements over the course of a few days. This pattern feels like a new kind of tool -- liquid software? -- and every application that doesn't have this feature now has a slightly rigid and anachronistic flavor. Why can't I just tell it how I want it to be different?

Now, it's not obvious to me how this pattern can or should scale. Does it become unmaintainable after a while? (Maybe model intelligence improvement outstrips my feature appetite such that it's fine?) How does collaborative software work in this model? Can software designed this way be secure and reliable?

Whatever the larger questions about broader deployment, it definitely works great in a personal context. It reminds me a little of the visions of Lisp/Lisp machines, Smalltalk, and HyperCard -- systems that the user can take control of and modify. Those visions never quite worked, though: the vast majority of software today is not end-user modifiable in any useful way. So, while this "liquid" affordance is a very small touch, the way it changes one's relation to the software feels a bit transgressive and empowering in a Lickliderian and Engelbartian way.

📝 New article on Our World in Data: Around half of people will experience a mental health issue in their lifetime.

How many people struggle with mental health issues?

International and national health statistics will often give us estimates for how many people have depression, anxiety, or an eating disorder at any given time. But people can develop mental health disorders at any point in their lives, or experience recurring episodes over many years.

What share of people will ever experience one?

A study by John McGrath and colleagues tries to answer this question by drawing on data from 29 countries and over 150,000 people across the world. By interviewing people at different stages of life, they can build up an understanding of how this risk accumulates over an individual’s life course.

They estimate that roughly half of the population will experience one of 13 common mental health disorders by the time they reach 75.

Depression is the most common; by the age of 75, one in three women has experienced depression at some point in their lives. One in five men has.

For anxiety, the share is similar, as is the gender gap. For substance use disorders, it’s the opposite.

In this article, we look at these estimates in more detail and discuss why the true share might be even higher.

This week, many of the brightest minds in the field of fusion physics gather at an annual conference to discuss the remarkable physical process that lets us develop a new source of clean, abundant energy. At the event, Commonwealth Fusion Systems experts will bring a new subject of conversation: details about how we plan to operate SPARC, our fusion demonstration machine.

SPARC is about 80% complete. Its first job is to generate net fusion energy — called Q>1 in scientific circles. That means producing more power from the fusion process than it takes to heat up the fusion fuel, called a plasma, so that fusion occurs. It’s difficult, with only one machine in the world reaching this performance level. At CFS, we expect to be the second to reach Q>1, and we’ve begun detailed planning on the best way.

“Because SPARC is designed to run well beyond Q>1, we have lots of room to maneuver as we operate the machine,” said Clayton Myers, Interim Director of Diagnostics at CFS, who’s slated to discuss our Q>1 approach at the American Physical Society’s Division of Plasma Physics meeting (APS-DPP). “Part of the reason we’re confident SPARC will meet this early performance goal is because we have different paths to success.”

You can read more about our plans, including two options for magnetic field strength, in our blog post about APS-DPP. The link is in the comments below.

Among other talks and poster sessions at the conference, we’ll also share our newest work designing the ARC power plant, the successor to SPARC. And we'll have plenty of folks at our booth, so if you’re attending, stop by and say hello.

GPU infrastructure.

AI inference and production deployment.

As an AI/ML Engineer, you must build these projects.

1.) Custom Triton Kernel
Build:  A fused RMSNorm or RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding) kernel in Triton, benchmarked against native PyTorch.

Why: Python overhead and memory reads kill inference. You cannot optimize what you treat as a black box.

2.) Synthetic Data Curation Engine
Build:  A pipeline using a frontier model to generate 50k complex logic traces, filtered by a deterministic verifier for training.

Why:  The internet is out of human text. High-quality, verifiable synthetic data is the ultimate training moat.

3.) MinHash Deduplication Pipeline
Build:  A scalable script that scans terabytes of pre-training data and removes near-duplicates using MinHash and LSH.

Why:  Training on duplicates causes memorization, destroys model generalization and wastes compute.

4.) QLoRA + TIES Model Merger
Build:  Fine-tune a 70B model in 4-bit on a single 24GB GPU, then merge it with the base model using TIES to resolve gradient conflicts.

Why:  Full fine-tuning is dead for 99% of teams. PEFT and merging are how you adapt frontier intelligence cheaply.

5.) KTO Alignment Flywheel
Build:  Align an SFT model using Kahneman-Tversky Optimization (KTO) on binary "good/bad" signals without needing paired preference data.

Why:  SFT teaches what to say. Alignment teaches how to behave, and KTO slashes human annotation costs.

6.) FSDP Multi-GPU Training Harness
Build:  A custom training loop sharding a 7B model across 4 GPUs using Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) and gradient checkpointing.

Why:  Single-GPU training is for tutorials. Production research requires sharding weights without bottlenecking the interconnect.

7.) Sparse MoE Routing Layer
Build:  A Mixture of Experts router from scratch with a load-balancing auxiliary loss to prevent expert collapse.

Why:  Sparse MoE is the architecture behind the smartest models. Naive routing destroys their latency advantage.

8.) Vision-Language Projection Head
Build:  A lightweight MLP mapping SigLIP vision embeddings into an LLM's text embedding space for custom visual reasoning.

Why:  Text is only half the internet. Fusing modalities natively is mandatory for 2026 applications.

9.) Automated Red-Team Fuzzer
Build:  An adversarial agent using tree-of-thought prompting to systematically find jailbreaks and edge cases in your safety classifier.

Why: Static benchmarks are easily gamed. You must build harnesses that continuously attack your own models.

10.) AWQ Quantization & Perplexity Tracker
Build:  Calibrate a model to 4-bit AWQ, measure the exact perplexity degradation, and benchmark latency gains in vLLM.

Why:  Quantization is the only way to fit frontier models on edge GPUs and protect cloud margins.

11.) W&B Automated Hyperparameter Sweep
Build:  A Ray cluster integrated with Weights & Biases that automatically searches learning rates and weight decays based on validation loss.

Why:  Manual tuning is guessing. Automated sweeps find the mathematical optimum for your specific data mix.

12.) Semantic Complexity Router
Build:  An inference gateway that analyzes prompt entropy to route simple queries to a local 8B and complex reasoning to a 70B API.

Why:  Unit economics decide if your AI product survives. Routing protects your margins.

13.) Custom Autograd Activation Function
Build:  A novel non-linear activation function with a manually written forward and backward pass in C++/CUDA.

Why:  You cannot debug a collapsing loss curve if you rely entirely on PyTorch's `autograd` black box.

14.) Speculative Decoding Pipeline
Build:  A serving setup where a local 2B draft model proposes tokens for a 70B target model to verify in a single forward pass.

Why:  2x decode speed at zero quality loss is the closest thing to a free lunch in inference.

15.) Arxiv Reproduction & HuggingFace Release
Build:  Reproduce a brand-new paper in <500 lines of PyTorch, publish the weights, the training logs and a teardown of the results.

Why:  Top AI labs hire ML Engineers based on their public repos and training methodologies not their degrees.

Hyperscalers basically have two choices:
- Host and serve Chinese open-weight models themselves
- Rent their compute out to frontier AI labs

Either way, hyperscalers price their servers after baking in massive hardware depreciation, future part price hikes, and their own profit margins.

Frontier AI labs have to take that already marked-up compute price and add their own margin on top. 
Worse, their API pricing has to recover their massive training compute costs, plus the interest and returns owed on the billions they raised from those very same hyperscalers. 

They have no choice. Their prices have to be super high.

On the flip side, tons of providers can host open-weight models. 
That creates a brutal price war, which forces profit margins down and makes running them dirt cheap for users.

Chinese labs probably know this exact math. 
That is why they are going all-in on building the cheapest, most efficient open models possible.

Taiwanese parents who moved to Arizona with TSMC are worried that American education is not challenging enough. One mother associated with the chipmaker had moved there because she wanted an easier academic environment for her son.

As writer Dan Wang (@danwwang) reported in the New York Times this month, the company's engineers have found that their kids consider American classes far less challenging than those in Taiwan, and that math and science classes are a breeze. This is causing consternation among these parents.

Wang Yi-ping was an award-winning teacher in Tainan, in southern Taiwan, and her husband is a manager at TSMC's Arizona plant. When the transfer was first mentioned, she would have nothing to do with it. Her oldest son convinced her to change her mind.

He went to one of the most competitive public schools in the south, where before dawn every morning chartered buses arrived carrying the best students from Tainan and the nearby city of Kaohsiung. "If you aren't willing to put in extra for scores, you're weeded out," she told Global Views magazine.

Before his ninth-grade national exam, she dropped him off at cram school. She had barely gotten home when the teaching assistant called. Her son had said he was going out to the convenience store and never came back. The school called at least three times to ask why he wasn't in class. He had stayed home.

He went abroad for a year as an exchange student, to Wisconsin, and when he came back, he said to her, "Mom, I found out studying is just one of the important things." In Phoenix, his grades rose, and now he asks her to pick him up late after class so that he can stay behind and ask his teachers questions.

Taiwan's results on international tests show the benefit and the cost of such an education. In the most recent big international math test, 44% of Taiwan's eighth graders reached the highest proficiency level, compared with 8% of Americans. But 61% of the Taiwanese students surveyed said that they did not like studying math, compared with 51% of American students.

Taiwan gets some of the highest math scores in the world by putting all its children into the same race, competing for the same test scores. Among the other TSMC parents in Phoenix, there is fear that their children will fall behind in that race. Wang Yi-ping moved her son to get him out of that race, because, in Taiwan's system, if a child is not right for that race then he does not have an alternative track. For her son, the alternative track was another country.

Revolut: Europe's most valuable startup ($200B) just showed the world its AI strategy.

Every company will end up copying it.

At the start of this year, Revolut leaned on the frontier labs. Its 2,000 engineers used Claude Code and Codex, and some burned $1,000 to $10,000 a month each. The bills kept climbing, and the returns weren't there.

So Revolut switched its default to an open-source model called GLM. All it needs is GPUs, which it rents from Together AI.

The results, by Revolut's own count:

- The bill is about a tenth of what it paid OpenAI and Anthropic
- Engineers get unlimited tokens instead of spending caps
- Coding time is down 60% and lead time is down 70%

That's the chart below.

Revolut still uses Claude and GPT, but only as "the exception," for the tasks they do best. Everything else runs on open source.

So here's the question I keep coming back to: how many use cases can companies really justify sending to frontier models?

My answer is very few. Plenty of companies still route everything to OpenAI and Anthropic today. For how long?

I think open source ends up handling the vast majority of corporate AI work, and frontier models get a short list of the hardest jobs. That's a problem for labs whose revenue forecasts assume unlimited growth.

If you appreciate unpopular takes, follow me @m0xt_ for more.

i mapped every month Jan–Oct by its top themes on US X trends. the chart looks simple. the reasons behind it aren't

▹ month by month

JAN: Maduro captured (Jan 3) · ICE shootings (Jan 7, Jan 24) · winter storm, 85+ dead · Indiana wins the CFP title · Epstein files out Jan 30

FEB: #SuperBowl #1 · 5.25M+ social mentions, halftime 1.87M · Grammys + Bad Bunny · "Epstein" #1 · Nancy Guthrie #2 · US/Israel strike Iran Feb 28

MAR: Iran war · BTS ARIRANG, 18.4M live on Netflix, ~110M Spotify streams day one · Oscars · No Kings protests

APR: Artemis II #1 · WHCD shooting · Justin Fairfax #1 · Gilgo Beach plea #10

MAY: #MetGala #1 · Kentucky Derby · Late Show finale · Knicks playoff run

JUN: Knicks #1, first title since 1973 · SpaceX IPO at $2T+ · World Cup opens Jun 11

JUL: World Cup, 148.2M posts, peak 8.9M in a day · US 250th · Spain beats Argentina in the final

AUG: Luigi Mangione #1 · Lindsay Clancy trial · Keffe D convicted for Tupac, #3

SEP: Charlie Kirk #1 · Clancy mistrial #1 · GPT-6 launch, only #43

OCT: #DWTS + WWE most tweeted · World Series, #WinOurWay · GTA 6 #1 · Binance hack #1 · Keffe D sentenced, only #24

▹ why the chart looks like this

1. SPORTS 10/10: it runs on a calendar. Super Bowl, Olympics, March Madness, NBA Finals, World Cup, World Series. every month has a final, and every game night brings back the same team hashtags

2. POLITICS 8/10: shocks, not schedule. Venezuela, Iran, Epstein files, the WHCD shooting. it only missed Aug and Oct, when sport and crime took the slots

3. TRUE CRIME 4/10: spikes, not seasons. Guthrie, Fairfax, Mangione, Clancy each hit #1 or #2 for a day or two. no case held a whole month, and the sleuthing crowd lives on TikTok

4. TV, MUSIC, TECH 3/10 each: they need a moment. Oscars, Met Gala, a BTS comeback, Artemis. AI barely trends in the US: GPT-6 peaked at #43

5. CRYPTO 2/10: X only cares when something breaks. the Binance hack went #1, regular price action doesn't

6. YEAR-ROUND VOLUME: the most tweeted US hashtags of the year are #WWERAW, #SmackDown, #AEWDynamite. weekly shows beat one-off news on raw count

the read: if you want reach on X, build around the calendar (finals, award shows, launches) and treat crime and politics as spikes you catch, not a lane you live in

Custom autograd, CUDA memory hierarchy, mixed-precision training (BF16/FP8), stride calculations, operator fusion.

Stage 11: Production Serving & Routing
vLLM/SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, continuous batching, semantic routing, complexity-based model cascading, edge deployment (MLX).

Stage 12: Open Source & Portfolio
Publish fine-tunes on HuggingFace, write rigorous model cards, reproduce Arxiv papers, public benchmark teardowns.
